claude.sample_unit: clinical vignettes (each run 20 times, 1000 model outputs per condition)

links.outcome: Rate of selecting expert-defined optimal treatment with vs without guideline grounding in prompt
links.effect: Augmented model chose optimal treatment for 50.8% vs 23.4% for un-augmented model (McNemar's p<0.001); kappa 0.31 vs 0.09.
links.quote: For 234 (23.4%) of vignettes, the model identified the optimal treatment, a result significantly poorer than for the augmented model (McNemar’s p < 0.001)

links.outcome: Change in model treatment selection when vignette gender and race were permuted
links.effect: Augmented model performance differed modestly across gender-race pairs (p=0.02); Black women significantly poorer than white men (Bonferroni p=0.03); base model showed no significant differences (p=0.17).
links.quote: In post-hoc pairwise contrasts using McNemar’s test, model performance in Black women was significantly poorer than white men (Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.03).

links.effect: Omnibus test showed modest but statistically significant differences across 4 gender-race groups (p=0.02); optimal choice 48.4% in Black women vs 53.2% in white men.
links.quote: In subgroup analyses of the 4 gender-race pairs, model performance exhibited differences of modest magnitude (Table 1 ; Supplementary Table 1 ) that were statistically significant ( p = 0.02).

links.outcome: Frequency of LLM selecting poor or contraindicated medications among top choices
links.effect: Augmented model selected at least one poor/contraindicated medication in 12.0% of vignettes; base model 10.8%; community clinicians 22-24%.
links.quote: Conversely, for 120 (12.0%) of vignettes, the model selected a medication considered by the experts to be a poor choice, or contraindicated.

links.outcome: Augmented LLM versus community clinicians and base model on expert-defined optimal choice
links.effect: Augmented model 50.8% optimal vs community clinicians 23.1% (McNemar p<0.001) and base model 23.4%.
links.quote: A sample of community clinicians scoring the same vignettes identified the optimal choice for 23.1% (95% CI 15.7-30.5%) of vignettes, on average; McNemar's p < 0.001 versus augmented model.

links.outcome: Output variation across repeated runs with permuted demographic inputs at temperature 0
links.effect: Each vignette run 20 times with permuted gender/race at temperature 0; performance varied modestly by subgroup, significantly for the augmented model but not the base model.
links.quote: Each vignette was presented a total of 20 times, with gender and race permuted (that is, each combination of male or female, and Black or white, was presented 5 times).

unlisted_practices: Incorporating guideline excerpt directly into the LLM prompt (in-context knowledge augmentation) to improve clinical decision support

links.effect: Guideline augmentation improved optimal top choice: 508 (50.8%) vs 234 (23.4%), p < 0.001; poor choices were not different: 12.0% vs 10.8%, p = 0.4.
links.quote: For 234 (23.4%) of vignettes, the model identified the optimal treatment, a result significantly poorer than for the augmented model (McNemar’s p < 0.001); for 724 (72.4%) the optimal treatment was among the top 3 nominated by the model; and for 906 (90.6%) the optimal treatment was among the top 5.

links.effect: The guideline-augmented model selected a poor or contraindicated medication in 120 (12.0%) vignettes.
links.quote: Conversely, for 120 (12.0%) of vignettes, the model selected a medication considered by the experts to be a poor choice, or contraindicated.

links.effect: Community clinicians identified the optimal choice for 23.1% of vignettes versus augmented model 50.8%; McNemar's p < 0.001 versus augmented model.
links.quote: A sample of community clinicians scoring the same vignettes identified the optimal choice for 23.1% (95% CI 15.7-30.5%) of vignettes, on average; McNemar's p < 0.001 versus augmented model.

links.outcome: race and gender counterfactual performance differences
links.effect: Omnibus subgroup differences p = 0.02; Black women performed significantly poorer than white men, Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.03.
links.quote: In post-hoc pairwise contrasts using McNemar’s test, model performance in Black women was significantly poorer than white men (Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.03).

links.effect: augmented model identified optimal treatment for 50.8% of vignettes vs 23.4% for unaugmented model (McNemar’s p < 0.001)
links.quote: For 234 (23.4%) of vignettes, the model identified the optimal treatment, a result significantly poorer than for the augmented model (McNemar’s p < 0.001); for 724 (72.4%) the optimal treatment was among the top 3 nominated by the model; and for 906 (90.6%) the optimal treatment was among the top 5.

links.outcome: optimal treatment selection disparity by race-gender subgroup
links.effect: model performance in Black women was significantly poorer than white men (48.4% vs 53.2%, Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.03; omnibus p = 0.02)
links.quote: In post-hoc pairwise contrasts using McNemar’s test, model performance in Black women was significantly poorer than white men (Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.03).
